A kestrel is a small bird of prey — meaning it is a bird that hunts and eats other animals. More specifically, it belongs to the falcon family, which is a group of fast, sharp-eyed hunting birds with pointed wings and hooked beaks. Think of a kestrel as a small, nimble, incredibly focused hunter of the sky.
The One Thing That Makes a Kestrel Unmistakable

If you ever want to identify a kestrel in the wild, there is one behaviour that gives it away almost instantly: it hovers.

A kestrel can hang almost perfectly still in the air — like a tiny helicopter — for many seconds at a time, even in strong wind. It does this by flying directly into the wind, spreading its tail, and making constant tiny adjustments with its wings to keep its body completely steady. While its body is still, its head barely moves at all. This is not something most birds can do nearly as well. This hovering is the kestrel's signature, and it is the method it uses to search the ground below for food before diving down to catch it.
What It Looks Like

A kestrel is a small bird — roughly the size of a blackbird or a pigeon, though slender and light. It has:

  • Long, pointed wings, which is typical of falcons and helps with speed and agility.
  • A long tail that it fans out, especially when hovering.
  • A reddish-brown back spotted with black markings.

Male and female kestrels look noticeably different from each other. The male has a grey head and a grey tail with a single bold black band near the tip — it is often described as the prettier of the two. The female is mostly brown all over with darker streaks and bars across her back and tail. Both have a cream or pale underside with dark spots.
Extraordinary Senses

A kestrel's eyesight is one of its greatest superpowers, and it goes beyond what humans can see.

Kestrels can detect ultraviolet light — a type of light invisible to the human eye. This is incredibly useful for hunting because small mammals like voles (a common prey animal) leave trails of urine on the ground as they move through fields and grassland, and that urine glows under ultraviolet light. The kestrel, hovering high above, can literally see these trails and use them as a map to locate where the animals are likely to be. It is a remarkable advantage that makes the kestrel a highly effective hunter.
What It Eats

Kestrels are carnivores — they eat only meat. Their main prey includes:

  • Small mammals, especially voles and mice, which make up the largest part of their diet.
  • Insects, such as beetles and grasshoppers, particularly in warmer months when insects are plentiful.
  • Earthworms, especially when other food is harder to find.
  • Small birds and lizards, though less frequently.
How It Hunts

The kestrel's hunt follows a clear pattern. First, it flies to a good vantage point — either hovering in the air or perching high up on a tree branch, a telephone pole, a fence post, or a power line — and scans the ground carefully. Once it spots something worth catching, it drops down in stages, pausing to hover again if it needs to recheck, before making a final swift dive — called a stoop — feet-first to snatch the prey from the ground with its sharp talons (claws). It then uses its hooked beak to kill the prey quickly.
Where It Lives

Kestrels are highly adaptable birds. They can be found in a wide range of open environments, including:

  • Farmland and fields, where there is short or sparse ground cover that makes it easy to see prey from above.
  • Moorland and grassland.
  • Roadsides, particularly motorway verges, which are surprisingly rich hunting grounds because grass is kept short and small mammals thrive there undisturbed by human traffic.
  • Urban areas, including towns and cities, where they sometimes nest on tall buildings and hunt in parks and open spaces.

They avoid thick, dense forests because their hovering style of hunting requires open skies and clear views of the ground.
Where in the World

Kestrels are found across large parts of the world. The most well-known species — the Common Kestrel — lives across Europe, Asia, and Africa. In North America, a related species called the American Kestrel fills the same role; it is the smallest falcon on the continent and is similarly famous for hovering. There are also other kestrel species found in Australia (the Nankeen Kestrel), sub-Saharan Africa, and other regions. In total, there are around a dozen recognised species of kestrel worldwide, but they all share the same core traits: small size, falcon build, and that defining ability to hover.
Nesting

Kestrels do not build elaborate nests the way many birds do. Instead, they are opportunistic — they find a ready-made spot and use it. Common nesting sites include:

  • Holes or cavities in trees.
  • Ledges on rocky cliffs.
  • Old abandoned nests built by other birds, such as crows.
  • Gaps and ledges on old buildings, church towers, and bridges.
  • Purpose-built nest boxes, which people often put up to attract and support kestrels.

The female typically lays around 4 to 6 eggs, which are incubated mostly by her while the male brings food. The chicks hatch after about a month and are ready to fly roughly another month after that.
The Sound It Makes

Kestrels are not silent birds. They make a sharp, rapid, repeating call that is often described as "kee-kee-kee" or "kik-kik-kik" — a high-pitched, somewhat piercing sound. They tend to call most often near the nest or when alarmed.
Conservation

The Common Kestrel was once one of the most frequently seen birds of prey in many countries, particularly across Europe. However, in recent decades, numbers have declined in several regions. The main reason is changes in modern farming — the use of pesticides reduces the insect population, intensive agriculture leaves less rough grassland where voles thrive, and the general tidying up of the countryside removes suitable hunting and nesting habitat. Despite this, kestrels remain widespread and are not considered globally threatened. Many conservation efforts, including the installation of nest boxes, have helped support their numbers in certain areas.
In Summary

A kestrel is a small falcon that hunts by hovering almost motionless in the air, watching the ground below with extraordinary eyesight — including the ability to see ultraviolet light invisible to humans. It feeds mainly on small mammals, insects, and worms. It is a highly adaptable bird found across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas in various species, comfortable in farmland, moorland, roadsides, and even cities. Its hovering behaviour is its single most defining and recognisable trait, and it is what most clearly separates a kestrel from most other birds you might encounter.
